item.title: Show HN: Run full iOS 16.5 firmware on Android Devices (367 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel, See on Hacker News

HackiOS boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel (xnu-8796.121.2, the kernel of iOS 16.5) on Android phone hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space on top of it: launchd → backboardd → SpringBoard → apps. Our own EFI loader, our own replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver on a compatibility layer make that possible.

It runs in two places:

  • POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood, Snapdragon 778G) — nothing is flashed: the UEFI is started with fastboot boot, the whole system lives in RAM, and after a reboot the phone is back in Android;
  • QEMU (virt, aarch64) — the same thing on any Linux computer, no phone needed.

This repository is half of the project:

Repository What
hackios-xnu-kernel (this one) XNU patches, the EFI loader, the UEFI port, Wi-Fi, QEMU scripts, xl, prebuilt kernel/loader/UEFI, common/ scripts
hackios-xnu-userland our init, injected libraries, launchd jobs, the APFS image builder, the scripts that take iOS out of Apple's IPSW, Metal/Mesa work

No Apple files are in either repository. ios165/fetch.sh downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's own CDN to your machine and extracts what is needed there. HackiOS is an independent research project by OOSEX GANG and is not affiliated with, authorised or endorsed by Apple Inc. iOS, iPhone and Apple are trademarks of Apple Inc.

Photographed on the phone, the Adreno GPU drawing (gpu=1). More in Screenshots.

What works

Works Does not work (yet)
Lock screen, swipe to unlock, home screen with all icons (two pages), stock iOS 16 wallpapers Cellular, Bluetooth
System gestures: swipe up (home, app switcher), edge swipe (back), Control Center Charging under our kernel (the phone only discharges)
Apps: Settings, Clock, Calendar, Photos, Notes, Safari and more; widgets (Weather, Calendar) on the phone Metal for apps (in progress: 293 of 456 system shaders already run on the Adreno, see docs/air.md in hackios-xnu-userland)
Phone touchscreen (Goodix GT9916), multitouch, wake on touch; real power and volume keys App Store content and Apple ID sign-in (no Secure Enclave; FairPlay daemon exits)
Up to 8 CPU cores (cpus=8), big core at 2.4 GHz, ~20 s to the lock screen Video and Live Photo recording
Adreno 642L GPU through Mesa/freedreno (gpu=1, OpenGL ES for CoreAnimation)
Wi-Fi (WCN6750, ath11k): join from Settings, Safari over Wi-Fi, 55–90 Mbit/s
Sound (speakers, main microphone), camera in Camera.app (front/rear, preview, focus, HEIC photos)
Data that iOS writes survives a reboot (var_store=1 ufs_write=1); iOS root volume on the phone's flash
Sileo + Procursus (dpkg, apt), tweaks, SSH

It is a research bench, not a ROM: a session lasts a given number of seconds, then the kernel returns to the loader and hands over its log.

Quick start: QEMU, no kernel build

prebuilt/ holds the kernel, loader and our programs built from these repositories, so all you need is the system image, which is made on your machine from Apple's IPSW.

Needs: Linux x86-64, ~12 GB free disk, 4 GB free RAM. Packages (Arch):

sudo pacman -S --needed git python 7zip lz4 gcc qemu-system-aarch64 qemu-ui-gtk edk2-aarch64

(Debian/Ubuntu: git python3 7zip liblz4-dev gcc qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64; 7-Zip must be 23 or newer — it reads APFS.)

git clone https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel.git hackios
cd hackios
common/setup.sh               # brings hackios-xnu-userland into the same tree, checks the host
ios165/fetch.sh               # downloads 7.4 GB from Apple's CDN and extracts what is needed (5-15 min)
common/build.sh qemu-virt     # builds the APFS images (and the kernel, if the toolchain is there)
common/run.sh qemu-virt       # a 20-minute session in a QEMU window

The lock screen appears after 2–3 minutes.

  • Mouse with the left button held = finger. Unlock / leave an app: swipe up from the very bottom edge; back: swipe from the left edge.
  • Keys: H home, L lock/power, ↑/↓ volume, F11 (hold) five fingers.
  • From a script: qemu/touch.py swipe 0.5 0.985 0.5 0.3 250, qemu/touch.py tap 0.615 0.71, qemu/touch.py key home; screenshot: qemu/screendump.sh shot.png.
  • Right after SpringBoard appears the system is still registering apps: give it 30–40 s.
  • Debian/Ubuntu UEFI firmware: QEMU_EFI=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_CODE.fd QEMU_VARS=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_VARS.fd.

On the phone (POCO X5 Pro 5G)

You need a POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood) with an unlocked bootloader, adb and fastboot, and the images from the section above. Nothing is written to the phone's storage.

The phone's own firmware is not in the repository and cannot be: it is the vendor's and is taken from the very phone it will run on, from its Android:

adb pull /vendor/firmware/a660_{gmu.bin,sqe.fw,zap.mdt,zap.b00,zap.b01,zap.b02} fw-gpu/      # GPU (gpu=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/wpss.{mdt,b02,b03,b04,b05,b06,b07} fw-wifi/              # Wi-Fi (wifi=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/adsp.{mdt,b02,...,b36} fw-audio/                         # sound (adsp=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware/aw8697_haptic.bin fw-haptic/                                       # haptics

(Put the fw-* directories next to the workspace. Wi-Fi also needs fw-wifi/mac — the radio's address on one line — and fw-wifi/network — network name and password. userland/build.sh prints which firmware went in.)

common/build.sh redwood GL=1          # images + out/redwood-boot.img
common/run.sh redwood 900             # loader into RAM, system image into RAM, a 15-minute session

or step by step with xl:

./xl enter            # Android -> fastboot -> our loader in RAM (fastboot boot); it brings up its own USB link
./xl ramdisk          # upload the system image into the phone's RAM (2.5 GB, ~80 s), once per loader session
XL_SECS=900 XL_CMDLINE="touchscreen=1 cpufreq=1 bootcpu=7 cpus=8 gpu=1 wifi=1 adsp=1" ./xl run
./xl screenshot shot.png
./xl reboot           # back to Android

./xl with no arguments lists every command (logs, screen and sound recording, camera frames, stop, state...).

Prebuilt boot image

Every release has hackios-redwood-boot.img attached: the redwood UEFI with our loader inside, ready for fastboot boot. It contains no Apple files; the system image is still made on your machine (above).

Building from source

common/build.sh <device> runs every step that this machine can run and uses prebuilt/ for the rest.

  • Kernel — needs theos in ~/theos (cctools and iPhoneOS16.5.sdk) and clang lld python perl. Details: xnu/README.md. 
    xnu/apply.sh && xnu-deps/setup.sh && ./xnu-build.sh -j8 -k
  • Loader — xnuloader/build.sh (clang + lld-link, an EFI application without EDK2).
  • Images — REST=1 userland/build.sh (variables documented at the top of that file).
  • UEFI — uefi/README.md (Project Silicium port); not needed to run, prebuilt/uefi has it.
  • After rebuilding: tools/update-prebuilt.sh refreshes prebuilt/.

Porting to another device

common/new-device.sh <codename> path/to/device.dtb   # profile + loader platform from the phone's device tree

Then follow docs/PORTING.md: the UEFI port, the loader's platform description, the kernel's drivers, the firmware. Device profiles live in common/devices/ (redwood.conf, qemu-virt.conf, _template.conf).

How it works

fastboot boot ──► UEFI (Mu-Silicium) ──► xnuloader (EFI application)
                                           │  stays resident: USB link (fastboot protocol),
                                           │  watchdog, receives the kernel's log
                                           ▼
            XNU (BCM2837 config as the base + our platform)
              ├─ GICv3, timer, video console, return to the loader
              ├─ APFS (images in RAM, iOS volume on flash), ramfs (/private/var, /tmp)
              ├─ minicrypto instead of corecrypto, AMFI and Sandbox stand-ins (MAC policies)
              ├─ driver replacements: IOSurface, IOMobileFramebuffer, AppleKeyStore, network stack
              ├─ input: /dev/redwood-touch ◄─ Goodix GT9916 (phone) / virtio-input (QEMU)
              ├─ GPU: Adreno 642L, Wi-Fi: WCN6750 (ath11k via LinuxKPI), sound: ADSP / virtio-sound
              ▼
   iOS 16.5 launchd → logd, notifyd, cfprefsd, runningboardd, backboardd, SpringBoard, apps
              ├─ our libraries are injected into backboardd, SpringBoard and mediaserverd
              │  (virtual HID services, a few ObjC method swaps — in memory only)
              └─ mediaserverd gets our CoreAudio output device (RedwoodAudio.driver)

The iOS programs, frameworks and dyld shared cache are not changed by a single byte: what they miss is done by the kernel (driver replacements) or by a library the kernel injects with DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES (kern.exec_inject).

Layout

Path What
common/ setup.sh (workspace), build.sh / run.sh (per device), new-device.sh, devices/*.conf, ugit
xl drives the phone over USB: loader, kernel runs, logs, screenshots, screen and sound recording
xnuloader/ the loader: loader.c (UEFI application), mkpayload.py (kernel + images + arguments container)
xnu/ our XNU changes: patch, new files, apply.sh / export.sh
xnu-deps/ everything for building XNU on Linux: setup.sh, tool wrappers, stubs
xnu-build.sh, xnu-env.sh kernel build
uefi/, mkxnuimg.py the UEFI port and packing the boot image for fastboot boot
wifi/lx/ the layer on which Linux's Wi-Fi driver builds for our kernel
qemu/ QEMU runs, touch input, screenshots, stack symbolication
tools/ recording (recording.py, sound.py), UFS/flash tools, mk-ath11k.sh, new-workspace.sh, host tests
prebuilt/ built kernel, loader and UEFI pieces (NOTICES.md for the third-party code in the kernel)
docs/ screenshots, checks.md, PORTING.md

Debugging

  • Session log: QEMU's stdout or logs/HHMMSS-run.log from the phone.
  • RC_JOBS=rc.jobs.tour REST=1 userland/build.sh — an image that unlocks and opens every app of the first page.
  • userabort: in the log is the stack of a process that called abort(); usertrap: (with systrace=1) — crashes.
  • Live stacks (QEMU): qemu/touch.py stacks NAME, then qemu/symstack.py LOG NAME (needs ipsw).
  • How a check can lie to you: docs/checks.md.

Screenshots

From the phone's screen, one session (GL=1 REST=1, gpu=1):

Licenses

  • No iOS files are in the repositories: ios165/fetch.sh downloads them from Apple's CDN to your machine.
  • xnu/ is a derivative work of XNU and is distributed under APSL 2.0, like XNU itself; prebuilt/mach.* is the kernel built from it. It also contains ath11k (BSD-3-Clause-Clear) and FreeBSD LinuxKPI code (BSD-2-Clause): see prebuilt/NOTICES.md.
  • xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libzbitmap/ and xnu-deps/build/lzbitmap/ — libzbitmap (Corellium LLC, MIT here); xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libdeflate/ — libdeflate 1.24 (Eric Biggers, MIT, COPYING there).
  • ath11k, Linux and FreeBSD sources are not in the repository: tools/mk-ath11k.sh fetches pinned releases. wifi/lx/patches/*.patch are our changes to FreeBSD headers; the rest of wifi/lx/ is ours.
  • uefi/files/Binaries/redwood and prebuilt/uefi/SILICIUM_UEFI.fd contain UEFI drivers from the phone's Xiaomi firmware, distributed the way Project Silicium distributes them for other devices; prebuilt/uefi/mkbootimg.py — AOSP, Apache-2.0.
  • This repository is licensed under the Apple Public Source License 2.0: our changes to XNU are a derivative of XNU and must be, and our other code here (loader, scripts) is released under the same license. Third-party code keeps its own license, as listed above.

item.title: Quad9 (DNS Resolver) to Exit France (1086 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://quad9.net/news/blog/au-revoir-france/, See on Hacker News

Back to Blog
October 22, 2026 blog

Farewell, France

We have some news to share with you.

Summary

Starting November 24, Quad9 will no longer be able to offer its free cyberprotection service to users located in France.

The French courts yesterday handed down an unfavorable ruling against Quad9 in a major case that undermines the transparency and stability of the internet. This decision in favor of beIN forces Quad9 to block the recursive DNS resolution for a number of domain names for users located in France. 

The good news is the court significantly reduced the financial penalty, from €580,000 to €1,000 per day. However, for Quad9, this has never been just a financial issue: it is a matter of principle.

We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.

This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.

Background

beIN, a Qatari company with offices in France, previously sought to force Quad9 to block resolution for a set of domain names they assert are participating in copyright infringement of its audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts. Quad9 has no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites. The French courts have fundamentally misunderstood the working of the internet and the role of the domain name system and have allowed a financial penalty to apply to Quad9 if we do not block DNS responses to users in France.

Quad9 is a Swiss public-benefit, nonprofit foundation established for the explicit purpose of protecting the cybersecurity of internet users. We charge nothing for our service and serve all people and organizations which seek to improve the security and privacy of their internet use. Our core values are to make privacy, security, and integrity available to all internet users, and our mission is to universally apply these guiding principles to recursive DNS resolution services in order to serve end users. 

We want to be very clear: we do not condone content piracy. Quad9 exists to create a safer, more trustworthy internet experience for end users. We offer global blocking as an option for malicious cyberactivity against users worldwide. We do not block content, and we give users the choice to use our threat blocking services, or not, based on their interests and needs. Content piracy needs to be dealt with at the source: the place where the infringing content is published. Forcing uninvolved third parties to break the fundamental operating principles of the internet to benefit individual parties to the detriment of the global internet-using public is misguided, counter-productive, and distracts from actual solutions addressing the hosting of the content directly, or the market pressures which cause piracy to exist in the first place. Not only are DNS recursive resolvers, like Quad9, the wrong actors to address piracy, but applying legal pressure to Quad9 will also have vast unintended consequences harming the cybersecurity of hundreds of millions of innocent internet users.

For Quad9, complying with this ruling is impossible. We have no database of users associating them with jurisdictions. Our service is free to the public and does not require sign-up or proof of identity. Recursive DNS is so fundamental to the underlying operation of the internet that there is no method to map users’ jurisdictions reliably, nor do we think there should be a way to force users to identify themselves before they can connect to the internet. Our core goals – privacy of user data and honesty of responses - are directly opposed to the methods necessary to implement the blocking this court ruling would require us to perform. There is no way we can determine which users this ruling applies to – we have no list of French users, because we do not keep dossiers of our users at all.

If we do not comply, we will face a daily penalty of 1.000 euros until the blocking concludes on November 14 (i.e., 24.000 euros) not including our legal defense. Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases, nor those of future cases similar to the one brought by beIN. Inaction is, therefore, not an option to challenge this decision.

Can Quad9 just comply via global blocking?

We could add these names to our global malicious domain blocking database, which is what we use to provide internet users with malware and phishing protection. This is a single, monolithic set of names applied to all users of our protective services (9.9.9.9 & secondaries) globally but not to our nonprotective services (9.9.9.10 & secondaries). Blocking these names for all users globally would satisfy the requirements of the court. 

However, this would have the “extraterritorial” effect of applying French legal decisions to every internet user worldwide, when they are meant to solely apply to France, for the commercial benefit of a single private, foreign-owned company. We suspect if other nations wished to impose their national legislation within France, there would be a strong reaction from French users and authorities. The converse is equally true: the findings of a French court are not applicable to the rest of the world. Such a system would set a precedent that any nation could impose their laws, morals, economic demands, or social constructs upon any other nation by the means of blocking DNS names, and thus blocking communication and content. 

Therefore, this global blocking method is entirely unworkable for us as a solution to be compliant with the court order.

What is “France” from the perspective of the internet?

There are more important reasons geoIP blocking will not work. We already prevailed in a similar legal case in Germany in 2021-2023 in which we learned an important lesson: we tried to use geoIP blocking as a “hack” in a similar circumstance at the start of the legal proceedings, allowing us to continue services in Germany until the case concluded. The plaintiff (Sony Music Entertainment GmbH) then used a VPN to access the blocked content from Germany in circumvention of the geoIP blocking. The court agreed with Sony in their assertions of noncompliance, and we were fined for contempt of court. 

From this experience, we know that the geoIP-based model is not only unfit from a technical perspective, but we have proven, historical evidence that using geoIP methods results in fines being levied against us by courts. To any technology-aware person, this seems absurd and outrageous – but this is what we face in these lawsuits where there is a disconnect between the courts’ understanding and how (and why) the technical protocols of the internet actually operate. We cannot risk this negative outcome in this or any other future instance, as absurd decisions apparently are de rigueur in these cases.

We eventually won that case against Sony, but it took several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time – all of which set us back in our ability to deliver services and is a resource debt we are still paying for today. This case is just more of the same – the opposition has more lawyers than we have money and time.

The decision of Quad9

Given these conditions and as a result of our unwavering mission, our historical experience, our desire to remain within the law, and the outcome of the court decision, we are left with an uncomfortable choice.

The demands lead us to an impossible requirement: we must adhere to the court’s decision, or we face growing risks to our existence. However, in implementing the blocking, we must either extend French law to the whole world (blocking globally) or create a vulnerability condition whereby we continue to be at risk because the available technical methods are imprecise,  impossible to validate, and do not meet any user privacy and security requirements.

This leads us to the only conclusion we can understand to eliminate our legal risk and keep us true to our mission: we must make our cybersecurity protection and general services unavailable to French users. Our departure is scheduled for November 24, 2026.

In any event, for Quad9, this is a matter of principle regarding the potential misuse of these types of blocking measures. Allowing private corporations to have the ability to block what is seen on the internet seems to us to be a dangerous and infinitely deep problem. Actions that seem reasonable and infrequent today will tomorrow become an avalanche of petty demands used to suppress political, religious, economic, or social outcomes. We will not be even a small part of that degradation of the freedom of knowledge. Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly.

This case with beIN is not the only litigation we face in France. There are approximately 20 different lawsuits pending against Quad9 (and other recursive resolver operators) that demand we comply with blocking hundreds of different names. We expect many of them to escalate to the same conditions as we have seen with beIN, which puts Quad9 at risk regardless of the outcome of this case. 

Based on the generalized, high-level traffic statistics we keep, we know we have many users in France. With our departure, those users will be put at risk from the threats we have protected them from for nearly 9 years. We deeply regret that result, but we have no other choice. Below is a partial list of the networks from which we see traffic in France. You will see many infrastructure, national security, finance, education, and other networks of critical importance in addition to ISP users and mobile users. All these users will lose service on November 24 because of the legal risks facing Quad9 in France.

What is the purpose of this whole lawsuit, anyway?

The most troubling part of this decision is that it is ineffective in practice. Forcing Quad9 to block domain names does not take the content out of circulation and has no effect on the servers that house the data. 

We offer a free service, and there are thousands of other open DNS systems that do what Quad9 does but with lower trust, safety, and reliability. Users seeking blocked content will simply shift their DNS to use one of those other free services, possibly using systems in other nations that have less-than-honorable intentions from a privacy and security perspective. This is like holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert. It is an unsolvable problem via recursive DNS, and the effect of legal rulings like this is not measurable outside of the amounts paid to lawyers and the number of words in press releases declaring hollow victory. 

Even beIN will not see any changes. Perhaps that is understood and the cruelty may be the point - we cannot say with certainty why such expenditures have been made against a small nonprofit like Quad9, which tries only to bring safer, trusted service to users. But of this we are certain: these actions are a tragic waste of time and resources and create a real, negative outcome for the internet community of France, whether or not they are our users.

What we are doing on November 24

Quad9 will not block the domains in question - we wish to remain committed to our integrity of providing a complete view of the DNS for users who wish that service. However, starting on November 24, we will no longer serve French users, thus keeping Quad9 out of danger from similar, perhaps even larger risks in the future. Our hope is that 30 days will be sufficient time for conversion, though we regret that this message will undoubtedly not reach some users in time.

An appeal is pending, and we will continue to legally defend our position in court in this case and as many other cases as we are able. We will continue to oppose court-ordered DNS blocking of this nature everywhere. Our resources are limited, but we are determined to keep the internet open and free. You can donate here to help us continue to deliver on our mission and assist us in the legal costs we incur in this and other fights.

What you can do next

We think this problem is reversible. French citizens: tell your legislators that looking up names is not a criminal offense. The internet needs to remain open and freely available to anyone, and neutral intermediaries like Quad9 (or any DNS resolver) should not be implicated in legal proceedings because we map names to IP addresses. Further, we know there are potential plans in consideration in France (and other European nations) to give private corporations and others automated and unvalidated abilities to filter DNS content that they alone determine to be unwanted, making it possible for a wide range of badly-managed or anti-democratic activities to be implemented. We believe you disagree with this as much as we do. Make yourself heard, or you will lose your rights silently.

ARCOM is your regulatory authority, and you should tell them this precedent places France at risk both from a practical and strategic perspective. 

Let them know that under their mandate, they have to balance your digital rights as citizens as well as the audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts of rights holders. Balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage.

In conclusion

Fighting piracy via DNS resolvers blocking is ineffective. It is disproportionate and misguided, ill-fitted and futile to fight piracy, as the source content remains completely available to resurge under another name. Forcing Quad9 to depart harms French digital strategy and sovereignty in the long run relating to security, privacy, and integrity - contradicting France’s supreme national interests in exchange for a short-term, imaginary commercial victory.

We deeply regret that we must leave our French users without cybersecurity protection, but we hope the future will see a more reasonable interpretation of the law which allows us to return.

Sincerely,

The Quad9 Team

item.title: MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada (243 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.cbc.ca/news/investigates/gambling-ads-restrictions-canada-9.7388888, See on Hacker News

This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.

For T.S., a 22-year-old Ontario man recovering from a gambling problem, widespread advertising for online casinos and betting during sports broadcasts is "frustrating."

"Imagine you're an alcoholic and there was a beer ad during every show you watched," he told CBC News. 

His gambling started three years ago as a fun Friday night activity with friends, but escalated. 

One night last year he found himself locked inside a bathroom, losing it all — having bet away $14,000.

T.S., who CBC has agreed not to name, says he quickly sought treatment and hasn't gambled since. But during his spree, all those ads fuelled him to gamble more.

"It certainly … would trigger me to go back and place another bet."

Politicians in Ottawa are moving to curb the widespread advertising currently seen across sports broadcasts, social media and online video games.

WATCH | Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There's a push to change that:

Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There’s a push to change that

Federal MPs are moving forward with a bill to restrict sports betting ads in Canada. It comes as new data shows that the number of problem gamblers is on the rise in Ontario.

The federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on Bill S-211, a law that proposes to rein in the ads across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.

  • Problem gambling jumps, suicides triple in Ontario after expansion of online casinos

2-3 ads per minute

A new analysis for CBC News shows Canadians continue to be bombarded with betting promotions during sports broadcasts.

CBC partnered with the University of Bristol to assess the 2026 NHL playoffs to count the numbers of logos and gambling messages.

Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages. Ninety-five per cent of those instances included no information about harm reduction or age restrictions.

Raffaello Rossi, the lead researcher and a senior lecturer in marketing at the University of Bristol, says by reviewing every second of the game, his team found ads or logos appearing two to three times every minute.

Ads appeared on stadium rinks, jerseys, helmets and during commercial breaks.

WATCH | Researcher Rafaello Rossi on his findings:

Researcher found thousands of gambling messages in NHL games

Raffaello Rossi of the University of Bristol analyzed seven NHL broadcasts and found two to three gambling messages per minute in the form of logos and banners, which he says are more effective than commercial ads.

"Advertising via logos around the stadium, on the jerseys, on the helmets is much more efficient, because you've got a lot of knock-on effects," he said.

"For example, if a news broadcast shows the highlights of a match, you will see these logos all across the sporting event. If somebody shares something on their social media, you will see those logos."

He says viewers are additionally seeing the emergence of ads for prediction markets. 

The new analysis also confirms little has changed since a CBC Marketplace study with Rossi's team in 2024 revealed viewers were bombarded with thousands of ads and product placements in five NHL games (up to three per minute). 

Rossi says that's because Canada is behind other countries in passing legislation to curb gambling advertising.

"Multiple countries since then have introduced quite strict regulations and restrictions on gambling marketing in sports. So, for example, in Belgium and Italy and Spain, there's almost entire bans on sponsorship during sports."

Proposed Canadian ad standards

If Bill S-211 is approved at committee next week, the legislation — which has already passed the Senate — would be presented for a third and final reading in the House of Commons.

"It is a national framework around sports betting advertising," says the bill's sponsor, Bardish Chagger, the MP for Waterloo.

She says limits on advertising are a way to address emerging harms, including growing rates of gambling addiction and suicide deaths, like those witnessed in Ontario after the province allowed private online casinos and sports betting in 2022.

MP Bardish Chagger is sponsoring a bill launched by Sen. Marty Deacon to restrict gambling ads. The standing committee on Canadian heritage is set to vote on the bill in late October. (Dave Seglins/CBC)

"People are being impacted in a very harmful way. They are losing their livelihoods, they're losing their homes, they're losing their savings, they're losing their lives," Chagger told CBC News.

Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate and says it is time Canada tackles some of the negative public impacts of online gambling.

"These ads are ubiquitous across the country, especially in national broadcasts that are sponsored by betting companies, with logos plastered across broadcast desks, arenas and fields; this encourages Canadians in every province to gamble, even in those provinces who have held back," she wrote in an email to CBC News.

"We know where this is going, but we're allowing it to happen anyway."

Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate, where it has passed. (Twitter)

Current Canadian regulations are supposed to restrict gambling advertising targeting minors, at-risk people and gamblers who have asked to be excluded from the sites.

But the code doesn't go as far as some European countries, which have outright banned televised promotions on sportswear and during events.  

Belgium, the Netherlands, the U.K., France and Germany have imposed time-of-day bans on gambling advertisements, restricting them to after 9 p.m.

In France, companies have to get approval for their promotional strategies from the regulatory authority and submit an annual action plan to curb addiction. 

While Canada's Bill S-211 isn’t prescriptive, it asks the federal government to acknowledge the harms of online gambling and hold consultations to craft stricter regulations. 

Toronto Maple Leafs celebrate a goal flanked by advertising for Jackpot City online casino. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Chagger says she hopes her bill will eventually lead to a ban on gambling promotions on sportswear and during live sporting events, outlaw ads during certain hours and prohibit celebrities and athletes from collaborating with gambling companies.  

Ontario and Alberta oppose the federal bill.

In a letter to the federal government, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction Dale Nally said the bill creates a two-tier regulatory system and threatens future provincial revenues.

Ontario's Attorney General Doug Downey wrote to the federal government earlier this year, saying that the province should be left to regulate ads.

"Ontario has already established comprehensive and modern regulatory framework for online gaming and sports betting, which came into force in 2022. Advertising standards and protections were a central component of this work," he wrote.

Public health response

A coalition of a dozen mental health organizations, including the Canadian Mental Health Association and Public Health Physicians of Canada, alongside 28 prominent addictions researchers, have sent submissions to Parliament asking for national action.

"The entire world is grappling with this in some way," said Matthew Young, a leading gambling researcher at Greo Evidence Insights.

"The real challenge right now is that we have a regulatory regime that is built upon physical borders, but a product that doesn't respect physical borders."

Addictions researcher Matthew Young is calling for limits on gambling ads and better monitoring of harms. (Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)

"The argument that it's provincial and territorial jurisdiction was all fine and well until ads from Ontario blanketed the nation and then suddenly New Brunswick had to deal with ads from Ontario."

The Canadian Gaming Association (CGA), a national trade group representing 80 companies that run casinos and online sports betting, has filed its own submission opposing the plan to regulate gambling ads across the country.

Instead, the CGA wants the government to spend money on assessing the "underlying health challenges" of gambling addiction, and let provinces decide advertising standards for themselves."

  • CBC Marketplace 2024 study of gambling ads

"Unlike alcohol and cannabis, online gambling platforms, both regulated and unregulated, are readily accessible with just a few clicks. In this environment, advertising plays an important role in directing consumers toward regulated operators that are subject to stringent oversight, consumer protection requirements and responsible gambling standards," the CGA submission states.  

Recovering gambler T.S. says advertising for online casino games should be banned or require warnings, similar to rules for other addictive substances, like tobacco and alcohol.

"I think similar to cigarettes, you could put labelling on the apps themselves, as well as the ads: 'Here's what happened to Terry when he spent half his life savings on blackjack one night.'"

    Axios reports that major U.S. banks, including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo, are detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts. In most cases the agent logs in with the customer's own credentials and permission, which breaks bank rules that require people to log in themselves. Some banks also saw agents contact call centers or take actions that appeared independent of user instructions, and executives say they often can't tell a human from an agent, or an authorized agent from a rogue one. item.title: eMudhra to Exit Global SSL/TLS Certificate Business (990 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://emudhra.com/en/press-release/emudhra-to-exit-global-ssl-tls-certificate-business, See on Hacker News

Will Sharpen Focus on Core Enterprise Solutions and trust services other than SSL/TLS

BENGALURU, INDIA, October 22, 2026 - eMudhra Limited (BSE: 543533 | NSE: EMUDHRA), a global digital trust company, today announced that its Board has decided to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business.

Mr. V. Srinivasan, Chairman, eMudhra Limited referred to the recent incident relating to its global SSL/TLS certificate and indicated that eMudhra handled the recent incident diligently, revoking the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovery and disclosing promptly. There were no end entity certificates issued out of the affected CA’s. Its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached. All physical and logical security controls remained intact.

He added that global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1% of the global revenue. Due to increasing data sovereignty & compliance requirements, complexity and cost associated with this business is increasing over the years. This, paired with the fact that some of the large entities issue the SSL/TLS free of cost, the business potential and RoI of this line of business also has considerably reduced for eMudhra when measured against our cumulative revenue base.

However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business. In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders. For many certifying authorities, SSL/TLS is the whole business. For eMudhra it is one part of a much broader digital solutions portfolio. We will put our energy where we create the most value for customers with Sharpened Focus on Core Enterprise Solutions and trust services other than SSL/TLS.

Seamless transition for customers

Our G1 RSA roots will continue to serve customers until this transition is complete as we work with browser programs and our customers to enable this transition. eMudhra will reach out to affected customers to replace any certificate free of cost from partners through the transition. Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. eMudhra will complete its remaining commitments to the browser root programs, including a full root-cause report.

Core businesses unaffected

eMudhra’s global SSL/TLS infrastructure runs separately from its other operations. The company’s Global digital signature certificate (DSC), eSign, and other signing services, including those in India, its enterprise PKI Solutions (emCA, CertiNext platforms), emSigner eSignature Suite, and its identity and authentication solutions (SecurePass, emAS) are not affected and continue to operate as normal.

About eMudhra

With over 17 years of expertise, eMudhra is a global provider of digital identity, trust, and security solutions, enabling secure digital transformation for banks and financial institutions (BFSI), enterprises, and governments across more than 35 countries worldwide. Its product suite spans CertiNext (PKI and certificate lifecycle management), SecurePass (identity and access management, multi-factor authentication and converged identity), and PrivaTrust (data discovery and consent management for global data-privacy compliance and DSARs), delivering high-assurance digital trust at population scale.

item.title: Crystal 1.22 (173 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://crystal-lang.org/2026/10/12/1.22.0-released/, See on Hacker News

Highlights

  • Standard streams emulate SIGPIPE stdlib/runtime
  • Revamped DWARF parsing for performance stdlib/runtime
  • All targets support native event loop stdlib/runtime
  • Support for LLVM 23 & 24 stdlib/llvm
  • aarch64-linux promoted to Tier 1 platform/linux

We are announcing a new Crystal release 1.22.0 with several new features and bug fixes.

Pre-built packages are available on GitHub Releases and our official distribution channels. See crystal-lang.org/install for installation instructions.

This release includes 251 changes since 1.21.1 by 33 contributors. We thank all the contributors for all the effort put into improving the language! ❤️

Below we list the most remarkable changes in the language, compiler, and stdlib. For more details, visit the full changelog.

Crystal processes exit immediately when writing to STDOUT or STDERR fails with EPIPE. This closely resembles the default behaviour of the SIGPIPE signal. Previously, the failing write would raise IO::Error, which typically prints an error message and exits. This error message is now removed (#17335).

You can opt out of this behaviour with STDOUT.exit_on_broken_pipe = false.

Thanks, @straight-shoota

Constants can have type declarations (#16951). They work exactly as you would expect the combination of constants and type declarations to be.

module Foo
  BAR : Int32 = 1
  BAZ : String = ""
  QUX : Int64 = 123 # autocasts 123 to Int64
end

Thanks, @stakach

The targets aarch64-linux-gnu and aarch64-linux-musl moved from Tier 2 to Tier 1. The only missing piece was that we were lacking official builds, but we have that since 1.19.

Process.fork had been deprecated sine before 1.0 and now we finally removed it (#17367)

Thanks, @straight-shoota

  • New macros enable more text operations at compile time: StringLiteral#bytesize (#17176), NumberLiteral#chr (#17169) and RangeLiteral#each supports CharLiteral (#17170)

Thanks, @straight-shoota

New constants Crystal::ALL_FLAGS and Crystal::USER_FLAGS provide access to the compile time flags (#17392).

Thanks, @straight-shoota

We completely revamped DWARF parsing to enhance performance and reduce memory usage. The DWARF parser now scans sections on demand (#17283) and builds an efficient index table once (#17410, #17455), which results in blazingly fast look ups. Decoded backtrace lines are cached in an LRU cache (#17285).

Also added aupport for DWARF 5 features DW_FORM_addrx<n> and DW_FORM_strx<n> (#17445).

Thanks, @ysbaddaden

We merged numerous improvements and bug fixes for HTTP.

  • #remote_address and #local_address moved from HTTP::Request to HTTP::Context (#17196)
  • Add HTTP::Headers#merge (#17326)
  • Serialize IO::Memory in HTTP body with Content-Length header (#17388)

Bug fixes:

  • Reject unrecognized HTTP Transfer-Encoding header (#17140), invalid Content-Encoding (#17262), and invalid HTTP trailer (#17337)
  • [breaking] Fix the return values of HTTP::Request#body= and #content_length= (#17257, #17273)
  • Fix HTTP.parse_headers_and_body to not raise with without_zlib (#17272)
  • Validate properties of HTTP::WebSocketHandler (#17235), HTTP::Request (#17255,#17304, #17374, #17310, #17312, #17258), HTTP::Headers name (#17317)
  • Close HTTP::Client on IO::Error during request (#17318)
  • Fix Content-Encoding: deflate (#17261)
  • Fix HTTP::Request.from_io parsing empty header name (#17254)
  • Fix HTTP::Request#form_params? to ignore invalid content-type (#17256)

Thanks @straight-shoota, @hahwul, @jgaskins, @Sija

All targets support a native event loop based directly on the system selector and use it by default.

We enabled epoll on Solaris (#17370) and kqueue on all remaining BSD targets (#17421, #17420). libevent is still available as a fallback, but now it’s strictly opt-in and becoming technically obsolete. We expect to deprecate in a following release.

Thanks, @ysbaddaden

We finally enabled support for Kernel TLS in the OpenSSL bindings by default (#17059)

Thanks, @ysbaddaden

  • File.exists? (#17307), as well as File::Info.readable?, .writable?, .executable? now receive a follow_symlinks: false argument(#17391)
  • Add Char::Reader.new(Bytes) (#17428)
  • Add Time::Span#to_nanoseconds etc. (#17190)
  • Add GC.syscall(&) (#17150)
  • Fixed backtraces when linking with -static-pie on musl-libc (#17316)

Thanks, @straight-shoota, @ysbaddaden

  • Uppercase instance and class variables (#17160)
  • HTTP::Request#local_address and #remote_address (#17260)
  • LLVM::Type#size and #alignment (#17494)
  • Support for LLVM 23.1 and 24.0 (#17432)
  • Updated markd 0.6.0 (#17269)

Thanks, @straight-shoota, @hertzdevil

Updated distribution-scripts (#17178) brings upgrades of package dependencies, docker base images etc.

Thanks, @straight-shoota

This is the first release featuring builds for aarch64-windows-msvc.

Thanks, @hertzdevil

Crystal established a forward compatibility policy in RFC 30: Building Crystal 1.22 requires a stage-0 compiler at 1.14 or higher.

Thanks

We have been able to do all of this thanks to the continued support of 84codes and all other sponsors. To maintain and increase the development pace, donations, and sponsorships are essential. OpenCollective is available for that.

Reach out to crystal@manas.tech if you’d like to become a direct sponsor or find other ways to support Crystal. We thank you in advance!

item.description:
See on Hacker News


Why brutal? Reads very reasonable to me, nothing personal and nothing about someone or feelings everything about the entity and its obligations.


"will sharpen focus on... trust services other than SSL/TLS"

Is there some reputation left to salvage here that I'm not aware of? Who would trust them?


They probably have cash in the bank and want to try to put it into something that might make money. An extreme pivot.


The customers for certs are technical people capable of seeing past that, so let them change it every day if they want.


No, the customers for commercial certs are mid-level managers, who believe paying thousands of dollars for something you can also get for free means you are getting a higher quality - or in this case even believe it is "more secure". Rebranding will absolutely work for that, especially when you market your untrusted root as "ISO-certified private dedicated cloud-based PKI-as-a-Service".

The technical people will just install a certbot and use the default Let's Encrypt config.


If they wanted to continue to make money, they could: exit the business, wait a bit, change the company name, and re-enter the business. Where "change the company name" could mean starting an actual new company, but with the same people, offices, contacts (OK, small problem there) and so on.


CA Forum, Apple, Google and Mozilla are to be blamed for just giving license to random no security background far away company.


Yes, its all very well someone here shouting about "the absolutely brutal question battery the Chrome team publicly submitted to eMudhra".

But in all honesty there are serious questions to be asked about:

a) The initial approval process for ANY CA

b) The ongoing monitoring process for ANY CA

The fact this CA was based in India ultimately has nothing to do with it if we are being completely honest here.

Clearly there is a fundamental problem with the overarching approval and monitoring process which means it could have happened anywhere. This time it just happened to be India.

Secondly, in direct reference to the "far away company" comment India does have quite strict controls on both certain technical things (speaking generally here, not specifically in relation to certs ... e.g. use of sat phones). And in general it is quite difficult (read: almost impossible) to turn up in India and do business as an external company. So there is probably a genuine need for an Indian company CA since not every body can/wants to use Let's Encrypt or whatever.


As a reminder Mozilla was warned not to add the Chinese government as a ca they pushed back claiming lack of evidence and only removed them as a ca once cnnic got caught issuing certs for google domains (by accident )


Not to give into conspiracy theories but this company might be ideologically even if not materially aligned to current regime in India. With right kind of nudge any kind business contract is possible without any competency.


Yes, not sure what the timeline was where trust was given to this company. Just horrible for the entire secure Internet. They've yet to answer many of the basic questions raised throughout this process too.


If anyone else also struggles to understand all the "4" references in the comments: One of their private keys was "4", with others also being in the 2-3 digit range.

Apparently they generated them like this: https://xkcd.com/221/


I think this opens bigger questions on who and how people get access to these capabilities. After that recent cold wallet physical supply chain take over, what sort of people are able to get certs for anything they need?


eMudhra is primarily used by the Indian government, so not hard to infer how they got into allowlists.


Terrible company, such evasive statements. Seems ripe for disruption.

Surely they should be investigated by the local regulator.

Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. On the day of the release, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC. Subsequently, from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified additional exploitation attempts of PHP2Shell targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors. Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.

The actual release of the embargo window was 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Two lessons from this event apply well beyond this one vulnerability:

  1. An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug. Coordinated disclosure is still the right model. But defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation. With PHP2Shell, compromise may predate the advisory.
  2. The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons. In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.

For security leaders, this changes several working assumptions:

  1. For critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours. A 7-day or 30-day SLA assumes a delay that no longer exists.
  2. Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17th.
  3. Invest in detections that don’t rely on a signature for a specific CVE. The first exploitation will often come before those signatures exist.

How AWS helps protect customers

AWS deploys multiple layers of protection to help safeguard customers. Our internal threat intelligence system automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability. We analyze over 200 billion events per minute and integrate threat intelligence from our MadPot honeypot network to identify and block known exploitation attempts in real time. Our honeypot system provides us with early detection of exploitation attempts, enabling rapid response and threat analysis.

Immediate recommended actions

  1. Upgrade immediately to the fixed PHP versions. Upgrading is the only complete remediation for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. There are no configuration-only workarounds that fully address both issues.
  2. Consider blocking multi-part file uploads in PHP deployments that cannot be patched immediately, but determine how this would affect your application prior to deploying.
  3. Look for POST requests with the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS string in form uploads.
  4. Review web server logs for suspicious activity.
  5. Check for unexpected process execution or file modification on web application servers.
