item.title: Several Linux kernel vulnerabilities accidentally posted to public mailing list (238 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.phoronix.com/news/LKML-New-Trend-Vulnerabilities, See on Hacker News

Seemingly as an accident, overnight several new Linux kernel vulnerability reports were posted to the public Linux kernel mailing list rather than the private security mailing list. The vulnerabilities have yet to be patched on mainline but at least in some cases there are patches undergoing testing or queued in "-next" branches. The CVSS scores are as high as 9.0.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative sent out a number of vulnerability reports to the public Linux kernel mailing list (LKML) rather than the typical private security mailing list. This seemingly was a mistake with Linux's second-in-command Greg Kroah-Hartman responding to each report asking about their submission to the public mailing list.

Among these newly-disclosed vulnerabilities include:

ZDI-CAN-33549 as a CVSS 9.0 scored vulnerability for SMB Direct remote code execution vulnerability due to integer underflow. For this one there is a patch in a Git branch of code intended for Linux v7.5 but now presumably will be expedited for getting to mainline.

ZDI-CAN-33774 as a KSMBD race condition that can lead to remote code execution. Another CVSS 9.0 rated vulnerability.

ZDI-CAN-33367 is a vulneravbility for skbuff skb_zerocopy in the network code that can lead to local privilege escalation. For this one Linux kernel developers received a security report from another source last week over the same issue and a patch is expected to be posted soon.

ZDI-CAN-34068 as a VMWGFX VMware graphics driver bug with an out-of-bounds write leading to local privilege escalation.

ZDI-CAN-34076 an uninitialized resource in the NVMET code leading to information disclosure.

ZDI-CAN-32005 was also posted to the mailing list a day prior for a search-domain TCP query stack buffer overflow leading to local privilege escalation.

The bug and security reports keep on coming in the AI fueled world.

item.title: HNInternal: Tell HN: I unknowingly broke the PHP RCE embargo. I am sorry. (322 pts)
item.description:
See on Hacker News


if you received the information about the RCEs without the information about the embargo, then you did not break the embargo. someone else up the chain did.

this whole saga will be analyzed and we'll all come out better for it at the end.


This is exactly how it works. People who are part of the embargo are responsible for making sure that anyone they share information with -- which should usually be nobody! -- are aware of and abide by the embargo.


you cannot be subject to an embargo of which you had no knowledge and took no participation in.

the embargo was already broken when pete received the information.


What does “take full responsibility” mean in the present context? Are you forfeiting all your assets and pledging the next twenty generations of your descendants into peonage?

(For clarity, I’m being facetious, but it’s a really meaningless and empty phrase to commit to the written record.)


>What does “take full responsibility” mean in the present context?

I posted something that -- in hindsight -- I shouldn't have, and it had repercussions for a lot of people. An action that I took had considerable knock-in effects around the world.

Some outlets are reporting that my action of posting something that I believed to be in good faith was an indicator or catalyst for the embargo to be tossed out and a previously-agreed schedule to change in short order.

That's not a normal Wednesday for me. Not even vaguely. I've not slept well since, and my taking ownership with an apology is this new course of action. Hopefully I'll sleep tonight.

re: assets and peonage – I am but a broke & wizened nerd with no known descendants. If you're ever in Cornwall, UK: look me up, I'll gladly buy you a sleep-friendly beverage. And I’m not being facetious.


Shit happens.

Years ago I lost $250K at work, well gave away, so real money out the door. I figured out why we were bleeding, that the mistake was mine (2008 vs 2009 in a function) and then changed the pattern to use explicit names rather than numbered events.

I figured at the end of the day I was fired. My boss laughed at me and told me good job for owning my mistake, fixing it, and then making sure it could not happen again.

Honestly don't just apologize - tell the whole story, in full. Tell us what you should have done differently at each step. Tell us where the process failed you and us. Those sorts of narratives and suggestions are how processes get improved. There is a humble and informative post mortem that you can write up and publish (beyond HN) for everyone's edification. But that should honestly be a Monday thing, when you have a clear head and some more perspective on the whole situation.

Honestly though, dont beat yourself up over this.


It does NOT mean "He agrees to settle any financial claims against himself or his employer, for damages caused by negligence".

Could have said "I blame only myself for this mistake, nothing else needs to change".

This will keep happening until the system where this can happen runs out of willing scapegoats.


> What does “take full responsibility” mean in the present context?

Aside from Pete's reply (see adjacent comment), I'd add that him taking full responsibility is also his way of saying his post was nobody else's fault but his.

In other words it's less about forfeiting assets and descendant peonage, and more about saying "the buck stops with me".

At least that's my read of his sentiment. Pete can expand if need be.


Don't be silly, you can't possibly be responsible for breaking an embargo you weren't subject to or informed about.


Not sure what you are apologizing for. It's a severely overblown bug that ended up on the front page of New York Times and the Japan Prime Minister had to get involved too. The bug itself is non trivial to exploit from just public requests to a web server so I am not sure what the hysteria is about. It's no different from the other hundred or so CVEs I see being posted or dropped everyday.

It will be headlines on Hacker News regardless due to sheer sensationalism, I think most DevSecOps people would rather find out the news here first than via their boss calling them after reading the morning news.


Well, consider that their old IT minister has never used a computer in his life, it's probably a good thing she's the one issuing the call to update.


Responsibility may include vetting your sources - is this person competent and dutiful, to actually know there's no embargo? - and researching the situation, and thinking several moves ahead, and other stuff.

Reality is that everyone has to make decisions in finite time, using the resources they actually have.

And I'd put a whole lot more responsibility further up that chain of contacts. And question how many other people they might have blabbered to.


>And question how many other people they might have blabbered to.

100%. I'm concerned about the two-way street this might also have opened me up to with information I shared privately with this individual. Nothing significant or incriminating, but the professional relationship is concluded.


Can someone, with the benefit of hindsight, explain the embargo ? Why isn't there a clause "if the vuln leaks, embargo is broken" . I still don't understand the fuss.

Everyone knew about the vuln well before the patches going live. The embargo, at that point, made things worse.

In plain english, please.


The modern version:

You have sinned.

Your penance:

Three Hail Claude's, one Our GPT and an act of loop engineering.

Two minutes of silent prompting.


It happens. Information cascades are messy, especially with multi-layered contacts

Thanks for owning it ,the best thing now is ensuring the patch details are clear once the official release drops. Moving forward is what matters


You’re setting a great example of how to be open and take responsibility, even when you’re not actually at fault. I really respect how you’ve handled this. You’ve also given the community a valuable reminder that some security disclosures may be under embargo, and that it’s worth having in mind before sharing.


Really hope you are not in the US. This kind of admission would be used against you in a civil trial, and lawyers love to sue for just about any reason under the sun. Someone could drag you to court and you might be able to defend yourself, but at an extremely painful cost both financially and emotionally. While I think that would be utter bullshit, that does seem to be the way this country operates now.


The parent is getting downvoted but he is absolutely right. Do not ever do what you just did. It makes you an easy target for a frivolous lawsuit in the US or in other countries because of the potential liabilities in your message, they are real. Even if you didn't do anything wrong, you are painting a target on your back, for no reason. I would ask HN to delete that thread directly.

You cannot foresee the financial/civil consequences of that RCE and some people might be looking for scapegoats in the future.


Sure it does. Saying sorry sometimes reduces liability risk, which is quite counterintuitive at first.


While possibly true in theory, in practice it's not. Courts and judges do not take kindly to frivolous or unsubstantiated claims, and any halfway good attorney would advise you to not waste your money and your time on a claim you are unlikely to win or be able to collect on.

People and companies do get sued with the full intention of a settlement and it never going to trial. But that only happens when the defendant has deep pockets or good insurance.


This isn't a matter of transparency, was the OP legally bound not to disclose the RCE? That whole "embargo" was pure courtesy between the people involved. The OP committed no fault at first place and the exploit was already in the wild anyway. Whoever really wanted to exploit it before the patch could without using the OP as a source.

> Anyone can sue anyone else for any reason.

And it's easier to have cause to sue when someone publish an "admission of guilt", which makes a lawsuit harder to dismiss thus costlier.

item.title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms (189 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://globus.software/blog/2026/10/16/cutting-map-polygons/, See on Hacker News

We have published the polygon triangulator of our map engine as a small library, earstrip, under the ISC license, the same one earcut uses. It is one C++ header, and a WebAssembly build on npm that takes the same arguments as earcut. In C++ it is 14% faster than earcut.hpp, in the browser 1.4 to 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js, and the comparison is near the end. This post is about how we got there.

A GPU fills triangles and nothing else. A map, on the other hand, is mostly polygons: buildings, parks, parking lots, the strip of grass between two tram tracks. Here are a few blocks of Śródmieście in Warsaw the way our renderer reads them from a map file, :

Before any of this gets a fill, every outline has to be cut into . Hover over a polygon, or tap it, to see what it turns into. These blocks hold 331 polygons with 5,151 vertices, and they become 4,514 triangles.

Zoom level 13 of our offline map of the Masovian Voivodeship, the region around Warsaw, has 3,740,425 polygons. On one core of an M4 Pro, the constrained Delaunay triangulator in our engine needs 2.93 seconds to cut all of them. This October I replaced it with ear clipping. To write this post I rebuilt the ear clipper one idea at a time, one commit per idea, and timed every commit on those same 3.7 million polygons, so each section below ends with a number.

Delaunay​

A triangulation of a set of points is Delaunay when no point lies inside the circle through the three corners of any triangle. Two triangles that share an edge are enough to see how the rule works. Drag the point D:

While D stays outside the dashed circle through A, B and C, the shared edge is AC. and the edge flips to BD; and it flips back. Each flip is a local repair, and a triangulation where no edge wants to flip is Delaunay. Of all the ways to triangulate the same points, it has the largest smallest angle. The orange arc marks the smallest angle of the two triangles, and the line under the figure shows what the other diagonal would give: wherever you put D, the edge the circle rule picks wins.

"Constrained" means that the polygon's own edges must stay edges of the triangulation, even where the circle rule would flip them away. Our triangulator inserts the vertices one at a time. For each new point it walks across the triangles built so far until it finds the one the point falls into, splits it, and flips edges around the new point until the circle rule holds again. It also forces the polygon's edges in, and at the end it keeps only the triangles that lie inside the polygon and outside its holes.

Well-shaped triangles matter when you interpolate something across them or run a simulation on them. A flat fill doesn't care: a GPU fills a needle-thin triangle as correctly as a fat one. And most of the work is spent on polygons that hardly need any. Almost half of the Masovian polygons, 1.8 million, have four vertices or fewer. A triangle needs no cutting at all and a convex quad is two triangles, yet the Delaunay code spends 419 ms on them, building each triangulation from scratch.

Ears​

An ear of a polygon is a corner you can cut off with one straight cut. Take three consecutive vertices a, b and c. If the corner at b is convex and no other part of the polygon reaches into the triangle abc, that triangle is an ear. Cut it off, and what remains is a polygon with one vertex fewer. In 1975 Gary Meisters proved that every simple polygon with more than three vertices has at least two ears that don't overlap. So there is always another ear to cut, and a polygon with n vertices falls apart into n − 2 triangles.

Here is one of the buildings from the blocks above. Move the slider to cut its ears one at a time, or :

The green triangle is the next ear to go. The algorithm needs one test, "is this corner an ear?", and the simplest version of it checks the corner and then every other vertex of the boundary. cross is the 2×2 determinant found in every geometry codebase; it is positive when c lies to the left of the line from a to b, so for a boundary that runs counter-clockwise a positive cross(a, b, c) means a convex corner:

static double cross(double ax, double ay, double bx,
                    double by, double cx, double cy)
{
    return (bx - ax) * (cy - ay) - (by - ay) * (cx - ax);
}
bool isEar(uint32_t v) const
{
    const Node &b = _nodes[v];
    const Node &a = _nodes[b.prev], &c = _nodes[b.next];
    if (cross(a, b, c) <= 0)
        return false; // turns the wrong way, or not at all
    for (uint32_t w = c.next; w != b.prev;
         w = _nodes[w].next) {
        const Node &p = _nodes[w];
        if (cross(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y, p.x, p.y) < 0 ||
            cross(b.x, b.y, c.x, c.y, p.x, p.y) < 0 ||
            cross(c.x, c.y, a.x, a.y, p.x, p.y) < 0)
            continue; // outside the triangle
        if (!samePos(p, a) && !samePos(p, b) &&
            !samePos(p, c))
            return false;
    }
    return true;
}

A point on an edge of the triangle counts as inside: if the ear touched the rest of the boundary, cutting it off would leave a polygon that touches itself. The one exception is a point at exactly the position of a, b or c, which happens where an outline meets itself at a single vertex. Holes make that common.

Holes​

Ear clipping works on one closed boundary, and 11,345 of the Masovian polygons have holes, such as courtyards and clearings in forests. The way to deal with them is to cut each hole open and stitch it to the outer ring with a bridge, an edge from a vertex of the hole to a vertex of the boundary, walked once in each direction. The boundary then runs around the outside, crosses the bridge, goes around the hole the other way and comes back. There is no area between the two copies of the bridge, so the polygon is the same, but now it is one ring.

The bridge must not cross anything. David Eberly's write-up of ear clipping has a neat way to find one. Take the rightmost vertex of the hole, m, and cast a ray to the right. The first edge the ray hits, at I, has an end P further to the right. If no boundary vertex lies inside the triangle m, I, P, the bridge m–P is safe. You can drag the hole around:

the triangle is empty and the bridge goes to P. the tip of the dent sits inside the triangle, and the bridge goes to the dent instead: of the dents in the triangle, Eberly takes the one closest in angle to the ray. Holes are bridged rightmost first, so a hole further left can bridge to one that is already part of the boundary.

Map data adds two cases of its own. Our coordinates are integers on a tile grid, so a ray along a grid line runs all the time; the crossing test passes over such a vertex, and my first version got exactly this case wrong. And mappers often draw a courtyard that at one point. Such a hole needs no bridge: the two rings are joined at the shared vertex.

The naive clipper (−1,812 ms)​

With holes bridged, the first complete version walks around the boundary, tests corners with the isEar above, cuts every ear it finds and writes each triangle as three indices. On the Masovian polygons it takes 1.12 seconds, 2.6 times faster than Delaunay. The chart splits each time by polygon size; hover over a part of a bar to see its number, or click a row:

is shorter than in every size class but the last. The 1,123 largest polygons, with 257 vertices or more, take 199 ms to clip and 90 ms with Delaunay. Each ear test there walks hundreds of vertices, and a polygon needs hundreds of tests, so the cost grows with the square of its size. The rest of this post is about making the ear test cheaper and needed less often.

Test only the dents (−237 ms)​

Look at which vertices can actually stop a convex corner from being an ear. Say some vertices lie inside its triangle, and take the one closest to the corner itself. Its two edges can't cross the sides of the triangle, so both run back, away from the corner, and the polygon wraps around that vertex from the corner's side. That makes it a reflex vertex, a dent. So if anything is inside the triangle, a dent is inside it too, and the test only has to look at the dents.

The engine keeps a list of them. A dent leaves the list when cutting its neighbour makes it convex, and a convex corner never turns into a dent, so the list only shrinks. The test becomes:

bool isEar(uint32_t v) const
{
    const Node &b = _nodes[v];
    if (b.reflex)
        return false;
    const Node &a = _nodes[b.prev], &c = _nodes[b.next];
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < _live; ++i) {
        const Item &p = _items[i]; // a dent
        if (p.node == b.prev || p.node == b.next)
            continue;
        if (cross(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y, p.x, p.y) < 0 ||
            cross(b.x, b.y, c.x, c.y, p.x, p.y) < 0 ||
            cross(c.x, c.y, a.x, a.y, p.x, p.y) < 0)
            continue;
        if ((p.x != a.x || p.y != a.y) &&
            (p.x != b.x || p.y != b.y) &&
            (p.x != c.x || p.y != c.y))
            return false;
    }
    return true;
}

The 28.1 million ear tests now look at 185 million points instead of 353 million, and the total drops to . That is less than you might expect, because building outlines have a lot of dents. The building with the arch above has 15 of them among its 27 vertices. And the smallest polygons get slower, from 34 to 54 ms: for a triangle or a quad, sorting the corners into dents and the rest costs more than the walk it saves.

Skip tests on convex polygons (−2 ms)​

A polygon without dents is convex, and every corner of a convex polygon is an ear, so it can be cut without a single test. Checking for that needs care. "Every corner turns left" is not enough:

The turns left at all five corners, because it goes around its centre twice. The engine adds one more condition. Walking around a convex ring, the edges go right along the bottom and left along the top, so their x direction changes exactly twice, at the leftmost and the rightmost point. The passes; the star changes direction four times, at the circled corners, and goes to the ordinary ear tests. Both counts come out of the same loop that marks the dents, so the check costs almost nothing. Triangles and quads get their own shortcut before that loop.

The shortcut removes 4.4 million of the 28.1 million ear tests, but those were the cheapest ones: a ring without dents has nothing to scan. On its own it barely moves the total, , though the polygons with four vertices or fewer win back part of what the dents cost them, from 54 to 48 ms. It matters more in the next step, where a convex ring becomes a single strip.

Write strips (−118 ms)​

So far every triangle costs three indices. A GPU can also draw a triangle strip, where each new index adds a triangle made of it and the two before. A convex ring makes one strip if you zig-zag across it:

The ear clipper can write strips too. Cutting an ear makes the corners of its two neighbours sharper, so they are good candidates for the next ear, and cutting one of them extends the strip by a single index. The engine tries them first and keeps alternating between the two ends while the ears last. In its code the neighbours of the cut vertex are a and b:

// The next ear alternates between the ends of the cut.
while (true) {
    if (sideA) {
        const uint32_t z = n[a].prev;
        _strips.push_back(n[z].index);
        unlink(a);
        a = z;
    } else {
        const uint32_t z = n[b].next;
        _strips.push_back(n[z].index);
        unlink(b);
        b = z;
    }
    count--;
    sideA = !sideA;
    if (count < 3 || !isEar(sideA ? a : b))
        break;
}

When the next corner is not an ear, the strip ends and the walk goes on from where it stopped. The 21.5 million triangles now take 35.8 million indices instead of 64.5 million. The ear tests don't get fewer: the naive walk already went on at the next corner after a cut, and now every strip also ends on a test that fails, 25.0 million instead of 23.7 million. Still, the total falls to , and the largest polygons drop from 146 to 103 ms.

Sort the dents into buckets (−65 ms)​

A forest or a lake can have thousands of vertices and hundreds of dents, and each ear test still reads every one of them. When a polygon has more than 32 dents, the engine sorts them into buckets along the longer side of their bounding box, about two dents per bucket. An ear test looks only at the buckets that its triangle spans. As dents turn convex and leave, the index is rebuilt once half of it is gone.

Points scanned fall from 181 million to 101 million, almost all of it on the large polygons: the polygons with 257 vertices or more go from 103 to 57 ms. Total: .

Count without branches (−178 ms)​

The loop in the dent test exits at the first dent inside the triangle. Most of the time there is none: the test reads all the dents and says yes. An early exit then buys nothing, and the three comparisons per point are branches the CPU has to predict. The engine first runs a pass that only counts dents inside the triangle, with no branches at all:

const double abx = b.x - a.x, aby = b.y - a.y;
const double bcx = c.x - b.x, bcy = c.y - b.y;
const double cax = a.x - c.x, cay = a.y - c.y;
uint32_t hits = 0;
for (uint32_t i = begin; i < end; ++i) {
    const Item &p = items[i];
    const double side = std::min(
        std::min(abx * (p.y - a.y) - aby * (p.x - a.x),
                 bcx * (p.y - b.y) - bcy * (p.x - b.x)),
        cax * (p.y - c.y) - cay * (p.x - c.x));
    hits += (uint32_t)(side >= 0) & (uint32_t)(p.node != ia)
          & (uint32_t)(p.node != ic);
}
if (hits == 0)
    return true;

The smallest of the three determinants is non-negative exactly when the point is inside the closed triangle. Only when the count is not zero does the exact loop from before run, to rule out dents that sit on a corner. The bucket version does the same with a bounding-box test, 64 points at a time into a bit mask. The total falls to , and the middle sizes gain the most: polygons with 33 to 256 vertices go from 327 to 216 ms.

Test only the marked dents (−30 ms)​

When the count is not zero, the exact loop reads all the dents again, although the first pass has already seen which ones were inside. The bucket version keeps that in its bit mask. The short list, up to 32 dents, can do the same: the first pass sets one bit per hit instead of counting, and the exact test looks only at those dents:

    hits |= ((uint32_t)(side >= 0) & (uint32_t)(p.node != ia)
             & (uint32_t)(p.node != ic)) << (i - begin);
}
while (hits) {
    const Item &p = items[begin + lowestBit(hits)];
    hits &= hits - 1;
    // the exact test from before
}

Points read fall from 128 million to 120 million. This is the last step, and it is the code of earstrip as published: , 6.0 times less than Delaunay on the same polygons.

When there are no ears​

Meisters' theorem is about simple polygons. Map data is rounded to a tile grid, and rounding can break a simple polygon. Here is the outline of Warszawa Śródmieście, a railway station less than a kilometre from the blocks above, rounded to grids of different size. The orange rings mark vertices that land on the same point as their neighbour:

per tile side, the grid our map files use, a grid step is 18 cm. Even there 31 of the 154 vertices merge with a neighbour, because mappers often place points a few centimetres apart, and the outline survives. nearly half of the vertices merge, and the clipper still cuts it. the rounded outline touches itself in a way that leaves no ear at all, and at 10 bits it happens to work again.

When the clipper walks all the way around the boundary without finding an ear, it drops the corners that have no area and walks once more. If that fails too, it gives up, and the engine triangulates that polygon with the Delaunay code, which still exists for this. In the Masovian data 76 polygons end up there. They come from a map built before the last change on the other end: our map generator now rounds every polygon to the final grid with GEOS's snap rounding and checks that ear clipping can cut it. In a fresh build of the Masovian map that repaired 273 polygons, and ear clipping can cut every polygon in the file.

Delaunay has one more job. Every hole needs its own bridge, and finding one scans the whole boundary, so a polygon with thousands of holes pays for thousands of scans. Our world map has a polygon with 11,675 holes: ear clipping takes 606 ms on it, Delaunay 17 ms. The engine now sends every polygon with 128 holes or more to Delaunay. In the Masovian data that is two polygons.

The library keeps both of these fallbacks inside. earstrip covers a polygon with a constrained Delaunay triangulation of its ring edges when the ears run out, when the triangles they leave cover the wrong area, and when it has more than 128 rings; run() in C++ and lastStatus() in JavaScript say which way a polygon went. On the 56,472 polygons of our world map tiles, with up to 11,675 holes in one, earstrip takes 459 ms and earcut.hpp 2,892 ms. On the zoom 13 polygons that the ears can't cut exactly, earcut's triangles differ from an even-odd fill of the rings on 31% of the pixels on average, earstrip's on 0.15%.

In the browser​

Before the new clipper went into the app, I compared it with earcut, the ear clipper behind MapLibre and Mapbox GL, in its C++ version earcut.hpp 3.2.4. Natively the two are close, and that could have been the end of it. But we are working on a web renderer that runs the same C++ engine compiled to WebAssembly, so I went further and compared the browser side too: both clippers compiled to WebAssembly, and earcut.js 3.2.4, the JavaScript original that web maps run today. For that I took the clipper out of the engine into earstrip. On all 5.8 million polygons of our test sets it writes exactly the engine's strips, and its repository has these polygons and the code behind every number in this section. Its native benchmark is the one behind the chart above, and the native row below is the last step run against earcut.hpp. Every WebAssembly build gives exactly the same triangles as its native version on all 4.4 million polygons of zoom levels 13 and 9. Milliseconds for the 3.74 million polygons of zoom 13, best of 7, one thread, V8 in Node and JavaScriptCore in Bun:

earstripearcut
Native C++489557
WebAssembly, loop inside the module, V8 / JSC601 / 566930 / 843
WebAssembly, one call from JS per polygon, V8 / JSC688 / 6881,007 / 950
npm package, one call per polygon, V8 / JSC766 / 8071,103 / 1,290
npm package, direct calls, all polygons in one call, V8 / JSC635 / 619

Natively earcut.hpp is 14% slower than earstrip. Compiled to WebAssembly and run in V8, earstrip loses 23% and earcut.hpp loses 67%, almost all of it in its main loop that searches for ears. It isn't the allocator: builds with mimalloc and emmalloc give the same time. I haven't dug further. In V8, earcut.hpp in WebAssembly ends up only 19% faster than plain earcut.js, and 10% once each polygon is a separate call from JavaScript.

The package rows are what a web page gets, and the earcut column there is earcut.js. The call that replaces earcut takes the coordinates as JavaScript numbers and returns a new array of triangle indices every time: 1.4 times as fast as earcut.js in V8 and 1.6 times in JavaScriptCore. About half of what it loses against the loop inside the module goes into copying the coordinates in and turning the strips into a list, the rest into calling into WebAssembly once per polygon. The direct calls skip all of that: the polygons go straight into the module's memory and come back as one index buffer of strips for WebGL 2 or WebGPU, 1.7 and 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js.

Some of the ideas above are in earcut too. It also relies on the fact that only a dent can block an ear, but it checks that last, for every vertex that passes the bounding box and triangle tests, instead of keeping a list of dents. Above 80 vertices it links them in z-order and scans only the stretch of that curve the triangle's bounding box covers, which does the job of the buckets. What it doesn't have are the shortcut for convex polygons, the strips and the count without branches: it writes three indices per triangle and stops at the first point inside.

earstrip is on GitHub and npm, with the polygons from this post and the code to time it against earcut on your own machine.

item.title: Jailbreaking the Switch 2 (600 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://pepsipu.com/blog/2026-10-switch2-jailbreak-ns2jb/, See on Hacker News

ns2jb is a software-only jailbreak of the switch 2 for the current latest firmware 23.0.1

Introduction

You can get a copy of the exploit from the ns2jb repository.

ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2. It allows running arbitrary native code as any ordinary sysmodule, and as the built-in fs sysmodule. This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2.

To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World. Thanks to my friends in Dabney House who helped me choose characters to add and playtest the game.

Setup

The very first thing I did was set up a harness around the Switch 1 and 2 so Codex could, ideally, jailbreak the Switch 2 without me:

Edit: Many people have been asking me if I actually used this prompt. No, it’s just a silly caption. I set a /goal for userland code execution, but that didn’t succeed. The jailbreak itself took substantial effort for ~2 weeks. The Mario Kart World, however, was entirely vibecoded in a day, and was just for fun.

The JetKVMs allow Codex to send controller inputs to the Switches over USB and receive video output over HDMI. We also need a way to press the power button—when the Switch 2 crashes, it needs a button press to restart.

That’s what the Bluetooth light switch flicker from Amazon is for. When the lever comes down, it presses the power button. Once the power button is fully pressed, the rest of the lever’s torque lifts the mechanism.

Getting code execution

WebKit is a popular target for console jailbreaks, so it’s unsurprising that Codex has picked it for initial code execution.

Code execution through the browser

It claims to have “native control-flow hijack” by taking advantage of a WebKit n-day loaded via a custom Wi-Fi captive portal.

We’d like to get code execution in microkernel services (or “sysmodules” on the Switch), so we can run homebrew, mod games, download saves, etc. Unfortunately, this approach of replacing one JavaScript function object with another doesn’t generalize beyond existing functions—we’d need a new way to make arbitrary IPC calls. That looks difficult.

Why?

  • WebKit has execute-only memory, or XOM, so even with arbitrary memory RW, we don’t know where a gadget that could perform arbitrary IPC calls is.
  • Even if we did, perhaps by parsing relocation data, it’s not clear how we’d construct a signed pointer for it because of PAC.
  • And even if we could, with some signing gadget, it’s not clear how we’d call this pointer, since CFI type-checks most call sites.

Codex has reset the goal to complete these steps. It’s a side bet; it may succeed1, but let’s be real: the accessibility of WebKit and the Nintendo BBP reward have probably incentivized many before me to look here2.

While that runs, let’s explore other options.

Code execution through smilehax2

My idea was to target Switch 1 games, for two reasons:

  • They’re built by developers. It’s less likely we’ll need to deal with PAC and CFI, especially because the Switch 1 does not support PAC.
  • Since the Switch 1 root of trust is owned, we can decrypt the code and read it.

Maybe we can still get the upsides of the browser attack surface—orchestrating from JavaScript, using existing n-days, etc—while avoiding the downsides of WebKit mitigations by finding a Switch 1 game that embeds a browser? Something analogous to Electron, but for games, so we could pull off an exploit like this Discord RCE. I can’t disclose this approach’s findings publicly at the moment, but luckily, there are other Switch 1 games.

In particular, I’m interested in SmileBASIC. This is because it’s been pwned before, in smilehax, giving userspace code execution on the 3DS. It’s a giant C++ codebase; surely, if there was an exploitable memory corruption in the BASIC interpreter, there can be another.

Codex found a useful 32-bit integer overflow in the interpreter. When removing items from an array, the interpreter checked position + count <= array.length, but the sum could wrap and become negative. To fill the gap created by removing elements, it’s supposed to shift the remaining elements left, like so:

memmove(
    backing + position * 8,                  // start of the gap
    backing + (position + count) * 8,        // elements after the gap
    (length - position) * 8                  // bytes to copy
);

Say we have a string array R of length 4, and we run REMOVE R,&H60000000,&H3FFFFFFF. position + count wraps to 0x9fffffff. As a negative signed 32-bit integer, it’s less than array.length. The multiplications by 8 also wrap, so we end up performing memmove(backing, backing - 8, 32), pulling the previous 8 bytes into the array. The command does report an Out of memory error, but it doesn’t matter, since the copy has happened already.

This is useful because the 8 bytes preceding any array in SmileBASIC contain a pointer to the array itself! After the REMOVE, operations on R[0] will treat the array backing as if it were a string.

Since a pointer occupies what would be the length field of R[0], the string length is enormous, and we can perform reads and writes out of bounds. We read and write to memory by copying to and from substrings of R[0].

This was a Switch 1 game, so the SmileBASIC agent could work on the exploit on my Switch 1, while the WebKit agent worked on the Switch 2. After some time, it got ROP.

Getting sysmodule RW

Okay, now we need to compromise a more privileged process. We’re interested in ordinary sysmodules and built-in sysmodules.

Which sysmodule should we pursue? We don’t have their code, so it’s unclear which sysmodules have which privileges.

I gave a few Codex instances the goal of getting sysmodule code execution. Most chose to focus on audio and ldn. I think that’s because audio and ldn have had bugs on the Switch 2. Codex also looked at the NV service, probably because GPU drivers are generally fruitful?

The fs sysmodule

In the meantime, I started looking at the built-in fs sysmodule, because:

  • The Switch 1 code shows that it’s able to serve decrypted code.
  • There’s a lot of code.
  • It’s probably similar to the fs module in the Switch 1, since the filesystem API didn’t change very much.

The first reason is the most attractive to me. Even if we can’t get a useful jailbreak from fs, we can at least decrypt some of the other sysmodules so Codex can find bugs in them. Other sysmodules like ldr and ro look enticing because they have permission to map executable memory3, but they don’t have large attack surfaces, especially from SmileBASIC. We’ll come back to them later.

Buffer overflow with path normalization

An IFileSystem handle has an IPC command, GetEntryType. This takes a path string, normalized with Path::Normalize.

Paths containing a parent-directory component with a backslash, like /..\, call into a helper that allocates a temporary heap buffer of 0x301 bytes. Our path is copied in, but it can be larger than the buffer, causing a buffer overflow. lol

We’ll need a good victim allocation to overflow into. Codex found that the BufferedStorage object allocates a cache entry for its files. If that entry has its dirty bit set, reads and writes to the file follow a pointer to cached data. We can hijack that for arbitrary read/write4.

From here, I scanned through memory to find SmileBASIC’s connection object and set the saved PID to 1. Now, my process has “FullPermission”, meaning I can perform privileged filesystem actions. I dumped internal storage and all ordinary sysmodule code, so Codex could perform offline analysis and I could understand where to go next.

Getting code execution as any ordinary sysmodule

Homebrew and modding typically rely on executing our own native code. Looking at the dumps, the only ordinary sysmodule with permission to map executable code is ro. All these sysmodules have CFI, PAC, and XOM. The interface for the module seems pretty minimal too. It seemed more fruitful to pursue a logic bug than to look for memory corruption in ro directly.

Let’s revisit that first point about fs serving decrypted code. This was useful for dumping the code for ordinary sysmodules. What’s the intended functionality of this interface? Loading programs?

Games and ordinary sysmodules are distributed as Nintendo Content Archives, or NCAs, containing a filesystem image called ExeFS. This contains a file for the main executable, main, and program metadata, main.npdm.

To load a program, the built-in ldr sysmodule asks fs to open ExeFS, and fs replies with an IPC handle to the filesystem. fs also provides two pieces of cryptographic information about the NCA header: the header’s SHA-256 hash and the developer’s signature of that hash. The loader uses this information to perform two signature checks:

  • Is Nintendo’s signature of main.npdm’s process permissions and the developer’s public key valid?
  • Is the developer’s signature of the NCA header hash valid?

Seems cryptographically sound to me, because, in theory:

  • the NPDM signature fixes the process permissions and developer key;
  • the key fixes the NCA header’s signature;
  • the signature fixes the NCA header’s hash;
  • the hash fixes the NCA header’s contents, including its filesystem hashes;
  • those hashes fix the executable content.

In practice, however, I’m doubtful of that last claim, because it’s the responsibility of the fs module to ensure the served filesystem matches the NCA header’s filesystem hash, and we have ARW in it.

Arbitrary r/w to native code execution

Indeed, with ARW, we can replace the ExeFS object behind the loader’s IPC handle with our own temporary filesystem. This filesystem still needs to serve a valid developer main.npdm for the loader’s first check, but the executable main itself can be arbitrary. The second check will pass because, by the time the loader opens the filesystem, fs has already submitted the valid NCA header hash and signature for the original filesystem.

There are two writes we perform:

  • The first puts a temporary filesystem object we’ve made into the domain-table entry for the loader’s ExeFS. This temporary filesystem contains the original main.npdm and our replacement main.
  • The second puts the loader’s ExeFS object into the domain-table entry for our temporary filesystem. It’s just to keep refcounts consistent and prevent fs from crashing.

These writes must happen after the loader requests the ExeFS filesystem but before fs processes the subsequent file requests. How do we ensure this?

The fs process maintains a list of its IPC connections. When a connection has a new IPC message, fs processes it. Using our arbitrary read/write, we can replace the handle fs waits on for the loader’s IPC connection with an event handle we control from SmileBASIC. That lets us control when fs processes a loader message.

With this, we can execute arbitrary code as any program we have a main.npdm for!

Getting built-in sysmodule native code execution

What main.npdms do we have? Well, all of them. With ARW, we can use to the loader’s fsp-srv connection to copy the NPDM of any ordinary sysmodule or game.

We’ll use this capability to launch our own code using ro’s NPDM. As mentioned earlier, ro’s NPDM gives it permission to invoke kernel SVCs like SetProcessMemoryPermission, MapProcessCodeMemory, and MapProcessMemory. In this case, we’ll use MapProcessMemory to create a writeable view of fs’s existing code. We can also dump fs’s code by reading this view.

These calls, however, require a KProcess handle to the process. To get a handle to fs, we’ll use our ARW to overwrite IEventNotifier’s 4-byte handle with 0xffff8001 and then call GetEventHandle from SmileBASIC. The kernel interprets this value to mean “the current process’s handle”, so SmileBASIC gets fs’s KProcess handle.

We can then send this handle to our custom ro process, who patches fs’s code.

Conclusion

Arbitrary code execution with any ordinary sysmodule’s permissions seems really powerful. We can investigate hardware without first exploiting each device’s driver. I’m hopeful this will help the homebrew community make progress toward CFW.

In the short term, there are a few next steps I think would be interesting:

  • Porting the fs sysmodule exploit to WebKit. Now that we know what bug we want to exploit, being able to perform arbitrary IPC calls is not as valuable. We might be able to trigger ARW in fs by changing the data used by WebKit’s existing filesystem code.
  • This jailbreak is tethered, and we don’t currently have a way to compromise built-in sysmodules other than fs. fs is a built-in sysmodule, so SM skips service ACL checks from fs, providing the same capabilities as smhax. I wonder if we can find bugs in other built-in modules?
  • With native code execution in fs, we can orchestrate its crypto hardware directly. For example, it’s used for NCA4 decryption.
  • The exploit has also been tested on the Switch 1, but I haven’t gotten around to packaging it yet. It wouldn’t provide the capabilities of a modchip, but it wouldn’t require any external hardware.

For now, I’m excited to see all the upcoming Switch 2 homebrew, emulation, and modding.

  1. It did not succeed. ↩

  2. It’s not inherently bad to attempt a WebKit exploit. Once we have a bug in a sysmodule we know to be valuable, it might make sense to go back and try to exploit it in WebKit with a data-only attack. This is because WebKit is accessible offline, meaning Nintendo can’t withdraw it like an eShop title. However, at this stage of our research, it’s not worth the cost to our iteration speed. ↩

  3. I wonder if one day Nintendo will map ordinary sysmodules and even game code via encrypted blobs only the kernel or secure monitor can decrypt. Then, no userspace process could observe any code on the system—there can never be RX mappings in userspace. Even the loader module, which starts new processes, would ask a higher exception level to load encrypted blobs it supplies. There’d be tradeoffs, like games being unable to read their own code at runtime. However, Nintendo has already started removing dynamic code features, like the JIT sysmodule. I wonder if this is the direction the Switch is headed. Luckily, that day is not today. ↩

  4. Initially, Codex’s read/write primitive repeated the buffer overflow on the cache object each time it wanted to change the backing buffer pointer. This hurts stability, especially when following many pointers consecutively, since each change is a chance to crash the system. We can use a similar trick to the one here. We can use some overflows to point the first cache entry’s backing buffer pointer at another cache entry’s metadata. Then we can replace the second cache entry’s pointer without risking more overflows. ↩
